Kenneth Starr. An independent counsel whose investigations into President Bill Clinton's conduct consumed American politics in the nineteen-nineties and culminated in Clinton's impeachment. Appointed to investigate the Whitewater land deal, Starr's mandate expanded dramatically to encompass the Lewinsky scandal, resulting in the notorious Starr Report that detailed Clinton's affair with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. His work became emblematic of partisan investigation and raised lasting questions about the proper scope of independent counsel authority.

Born in 1946, Starr was a federal judge and solicitor general before being appointed independent counsel in 1994. He was initially tasked with investigating Whitewater, a controversial nineteen-eighties land investment involving the Clintons in Arkansas. His investigation broadened to include questions of Clinton's financial conduct, obstruction of justice, and personal behavior. He pursued aggressive legal tactics including grand jury testimony from presidential advisors and threatened legal action against the president. In 1997, after receiving a tip, he expanded into investigating Clinton's relationship with Monica Lewinsky, making the scandal the focus of his entire inquiry. In September 1998, Starr released the Starr Report, an explicit four-hundred-forty-five-page document detailing Clinton's affair that was published on the internet. The document became public in a way that defined media coverage and public debate for months. The report's release and contents became deeply controversial, raising fundamental questions about how independent investigations should handle sensitive personal matters and whether statutory authority to investigate financial matters justified investigations into an elected official's private life. The scandal and Starr's prosecution of it ultimately triggered Clinton's impeachment by the House, though the Senate did not convict him.
